analysis.one_liner: Toughens penalties on opioid manufacturers and requires federal review of drug TV ads.
analysis.headline: S. 2440 was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in February 2018 and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill was written during the opioid epidemic to make prescription opioid manufacturers face real consequences. It would require federal health officials to review television ads for controlled substances before they air, raise the civil fine for opioid makers that fail to report suspicious orders or control diversion from $10,000 to $100,000, raise the related criminal fine cap to $500,000, and publish the prior criminal conviction records of opioid manufacturers every year. It would also fund DEA diversion investigators and create heroin enforcement teams with $50 million in the first year.
analysis.who_benefits: People in communities hit hard by the opioid epidemic, who would benefit from stricter control over how opioids are marketed and distributed, and from published records showing which manufacturers have prior criminal convictions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities affected by the opioid epidemic

how_it_helps.text: Requires television advertisements for controlled substances to be submitted to and reviewed by the Secretary of Health and Human Services before they can be aired, with violations treated as a prohibited act under federal food and drug law [S3].

Raises the civil penalty for an opioid manufacturer's failure to report suspicious orders or maintain controls against diversion from a $10,000 maximum to a $100,000 maximum, and raises the related criminal fine cap to $500,000 [S3].
Requires the Drug Enforcement Administration to publish the prior federal and state criminal conviction records of opioid manufacturers annually in the Federal Register and online [S3].

Authorizes funding for DEA diversion investigators and tactical diversion squads, and directs the Attorney General to create heroin enforcement groups to dismantle trafficking organizations, with $50 million authorized for fiscal year 2019 [S3].
Preserves the right of states to enforce their own consumer protection statutes against violators [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Opioid manufacturers, who would face fines up to ten times higher for diversion-related violations, a federal review layer on their television advertising, and annual publication of their companies' conviction records.

drawbacks.text: The $50 million for heroin enforcement groups is enforcement-focused spending; some members of Congress and public health advocates have argued during the epidemic that comparable money spent on treatment and recovery reaches more people, though this bill did not draw that debate because it never advanced [S3].

The bill raises penalties only for opioid-specific reporting and diversion violations and leaves the $10,000 civil penalty cap in place for other controlled-substance violations, and the $500,000 criminal fine cap remains small relative to large manufacturers' revenues [S3].

The authorizations for FDA ad-review staffing and DEA diversion funding are 'such sums as may be necessary' language, which depends on future appropriations and does not guarantee the money is actually provided [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow, targeted response to a documented problem: prescription opioids marketed aggressively while manufacturers under-reported suspicious orders. The direct costs fall on a specific industry rather than taxpayers or consumers, and the transparency provision costs almost nothing. Its limits are that the penalties, while ten times larger, are still modest for large pharmaceutical companies, and the enforcement funding is not guaranteed by the bill itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Maria Cantwell introduced the bill on February 15, 2018, joined by Senator Kamala Harris [S3].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
No further action was taken on the bill for the remainder of the 115th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid manufacturers avoided the higher diversion fines, mandatory pre-airing ad review, and annual publication of their conviction records. No other group gained, since the bill's enforcement and transparency measures also went unused.

for.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise opioid manufacturer penalties, require pre-airing review of controlled-substance TV ads, and publish manufacturers' conviction records.

for.name: Sen. Kamala Harris
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as the bill's sole cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup or reported the bill out after its February 2018 referral, leaving it with no floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic sponsorship (two senators) and no recorded opposition votes, so no partisan split can be measured; it simply never reached the committee or floor stage where votes would have shown one.

industries.note: The bill multiplies their civil fine exposure for diversion-related violations by ten, caps the matching criminal fine at $500,000, forces federal review of their TV ads before airing, and publishes their companies' criminal conviction records annually. Their interest in stopping the bill ran against the public's interest in controlling opioid diversion. [S3]

The pre-dissemination review requirement adds a government review step for controlled-substance commercials, delaying or blocking some ads, though the bill preserves state consumer-protection enforcement and authorizes $5 million to speed FDA reviews. [S3]
